issues.legal_issue: Property genuinely acquired and possessed by a third party, which was never owned by the judgment debtor, cannot be proceeded against to satisfy the judgment debtor’s decree.
material_facts: The objector relied on a registered transaction with the judgment debtor’s wife, paid consideration, and was put in physical possession of the property.
The judgment debtor had not held title or possession of the property; the decree holder relied on an alleged agreement with the judgment debtor.

The objector’s transaction documents were registered, while the decree holder’s asserted transaction documents were unregistered, and the decree against the judgment debtor had been obtained without a proper contest.
issues.conclusion: The objection was allowed, and the decree could be executed against other assets but not against the property in question.
issues.legal_principle: In execution proceedings, a third party’s claim to property must be assessed on its evidence and circumstances. Registered documents concerning an interest in property have greater probative value than unregistered documents, and property that did not belong to the judgment debtor cannot be attached to satisfy that debtor’s decree. The Court applied Order XXI Rule 58 CPC and considered the principles reflected in Brahmdeo Chaudhary v. Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal, Shreenath v. Rajesh, and Tanzeem-e-sufia v. Bibi Haliman.

rule.if: execution_objection_case and objector_is_third_party and genuine_prior_property_transaction and objector_has_possession and judgment_debtor_never_owned_property

predicates.execution_objection_case: The dispute arises from an objection to property being proceeded against in execution of a decree.
predicates.objector_is_third_party: The person objecting to execution was not a party to the underlying decree and asserted an independent interest in the property.
predicates.genuine_prior_property_transaction: The objector relied on a genuine transaction concerning the property that predated the attempt to execute against it.
predicates.objector_has_possession: The objector had been put in possession of the property under the asserted transaction.
predicates.judgment_debtor_never_owned_property: The judgment debtor had never held title to or possession of the property.

issues.definition: When a third party in an execution objection establishes a genuine prior transaction and possession of property that the judgment debtor never owned, the property is excluded from execution.

issues.legal_issue: A prospective ruling concerning transactions made through powers of attorney does not invalidate an earlier genuine transaction.
material_facts: The objector relied on a genuine registered power-of-attorney transaction made before the Supreme Court’s ruling in Suraj Lamp and Industries Private Limited (2).
The lower courts relied on the earlier Suraj Lamp ruling to reject the objector’s claim.
issues.conclusion: The later ruling in Suraj Lamp did not affect the validity of the earlier genuine transaction, and the lower courts had wrongly applied it to that transaction.
issues.legal_principle: Suraj Lamp and Industries Private Limited (2) v. State of Haryana, (2012) 1 SCC 656, stated that its observations were not intended to affect genuine sale-agreement and power-of-attorney transactions and that its operation was prospective.

predicates.appeal_from_execution_objection: The proceeding is an appeal arising from the rejection of an objection to execution against property.
predicates.genuine_transaction_predates_prospective: The transaction relied on by the objector was genuine and occurred before the later ruling took effect.
predicates.transaction_is_within_genuine_transactio: The transaction was a bona fide arrangement of the kind the later ruling expressly left unaffected.

issues.definition: A genuine transaction made before a prospective ruling and within its stated protection is not invalidated by that ruling.

issues.legal_issue: Execution courts must comprehensively determine a third party’s objection concerning an independent claim to property rather than reject it without proper consideration.
material_facts: The objector brought an objection under Order XXI Rule 58 CPC, claiming an independent interest in property sought to be attached for a money decree.
The objection raised questions about the objector’s transaction, possession, and the judgment debtor’s lack of title to the property.
The executing court rejected the objection by relying on the proposition that a power of attorney did not confer ownership, without adequately determining the issues raised.
issues.conclusion: The objection required determination on its merits; the lower courts’ cursory rejection was erroneous, and the objection was allowed without setting aside the underlying decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXI Rules 58 and 97 to 104 CPC require questions arising in execution to be determined in the execution proceedings rather than by a separate suit. The Court relied on Brahmdeo Chaudhary v. Rishikesh Prasad Jaiswal, Shreenath v. Rajesh, and Tanzeem-e-sufia v. Bibi Haliman, and noted that Rule 103 gives specified orders the force and appealability of a decree.

predicates.execution_objection_case: The proceeding concerns an objection raised during execution of a decree.
predicates.objection_raises_independent_property_cl: The objector asserts an interest in the property distinct from the judgment debtor’s interest.
predicates.objection_not_comprehensively_examined: The execution court has not adequately assessed the material facts and evidence bearing on the objection.

issues.definition: When an execution objection raises an independent property claim and has not been fully examined, the execution court must determine it on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant’s nonappearance or failure to file a written statement does not automatically entitle a claimant to a decree.
material_facts: The underlying money suit proceeded ex parte after the defendant stopped appearing.
The trial court accepted the alleged payment without insisting on proof, and the defendant’s wife, who was said to hold title to the property, had not been impleaded.
The decree holder’s claim and supporting evidence had not been scrutinized sufficiently, and no appeal had tested the decree.
issues.conclusion: The trial court remained obliged to satisfy itself that the claim was proved and legally justified; nonappearance did not warrant an automatic decree.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VIII Rule 10 and Order IX CPC, the court must diligently ensure that the plaint is proved and that the relief sought is justified, even when the defendant fails to file a written statement or is proceeded against ex parte. The Court relied on Shantilal Gulabchand Mutha v. Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company Limited, (2013) 4 SCC 396.

predicates.civil_claim_proceeding: The proceeding is a civil claim for relief by a plaintiff against a defendant.
predicates.defendant_fails_to_appear_or_file_writte: The defendant does not participate fully, including by failing to appear or file a written statement.
predicates.claim_not_proved_by_sufficient_evidence: The plaintiff has not established the factual and legal basis for the relief with sufficient evidence.

issues.definition: When a defendant defaults and the claim lacks sufficient proof, the court must assess the claim rather than grant relief automatically.

issues.legal_issue: A contractual stipulation requiring payment of twice the earnest money is not recoverable as damages unless it represents reasonable compensation rather than a penalty.
material_facts: The agreement relied on in the underlying money suit stipulated payment of twice the earnest money upon breach.

The trial court accepted the alleged earnest-money payment without requiring proof, and the plaintiff provided no evidence that the doubled sum was a fair pre-estimate of likely loss or that damages had been suffered.
The alleged contracting defendant was found to lack title to the property that was the subject of the agreement.
issues.conclusion: Justice Vikramajit Sen held that the stipulated doubled amount ought not to have been decreed because the claim was unsupported by proof of damages and the stipulated sum was facially penal; the appeal itself left the underlying decree undisturbed while allowing the property objection.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act require reasonable compensation for breach, subject to the stipulated maximum; a penalty is not automatically recoverable. The Court relied principally on Sir Chunilal V. Mehta & Sons Ltd. v. Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd., AIR 1962 SC 1314, and Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass, AIR 1963 SC 1405, and referred to Phulchand Exports Ltd. v. O.O.O. Patriot, Maula Bux v. Union of India, Union of India v. Raman Iron Foundry, and BSNL v. Reliance Communication Ltd. as consistent with that position.

predicates.contract_damages_claim: The proceeding includes a claim for money said to be due upon breach of a contract.
predicates.breach_triggers_stipulated_double_paymen: The contract stipulates payment of twice an amount received if the contract is not performed.
predicates.no_proof_of_reasonable_compensation: There is no evidence that the stipulated sum reasonably estimates likely loss or that compensable loss was suffered.

issues.definition: Where breach of contract triggers a stipulated doubled payment but no evidence shows it to be reasonable compensation, the stipulated penalty is not recoverable as claimed.
